THE CORRECT GUARD ALREADY EXISTS ONE DIRECTORY OVER: the canvas path carries sidecarRejected with the rule stated in its own comment — a sidecar Aurora could not READ is one it must not overwrite. title: A drag in progress survives a keyboard act switch and writes the old act's coordinates into an unrelated object in the new one, once per mouse move and outside undo.
detail: Controller-verified links: App.tsx:159 is a WINDOW keydown (key 1-9, no shift/alt) calling requestFocusIndex, so no pointer event is involved; the level pane at App.tsx:273 is an UN-KEYED div that only toggles display, so MapViewport is never remounted; getSectionByIndex resolves the act fresh at call time. Two damages: per-mousemove writes to section.objects[index].x/y with bumpLiveEdit and no command at all, and then finishGesture writes act A's start coordinates into act B's object through a real move-object command, losing act A's move. THE CURE IS ALREADY IN THIS FILE ON THE OTHER AXIS: endGuideDrag carries a witness (JSON.stringify(layer) !== drag.witness -> return, MapViewport.tsx:2450) whose docblock states the rule. dragTarget, paintStroke.sectionIndex, marqueeDragStart.sectionIndex and bandStamp all carry a bare index with no witness. And App.tsx:312 keys the CANVAS pane by document with a comment naming in-flight gestures as the reason; the level pane is the one surface that skipped it.

title: A tab switch that changes facet unmounts the map mid-stroke, so the paint is already written into the document but no command is ever recorded.

The window-mouseup effect's cleanup removes listeners only and never calls finishGesture, so the release never commits. This is the state MapViewport.tsx:2189-2192 says was fixed for the mouseleave route; the unmount route was not closed. A second no-pointer trigger is MapViewport.tsx:1835, switchFacet('art') from the keydown handler itself.

title: Ctrl+Delete and Alt+Backspace destroy the selected object, because the only data-destroying key branch sits above the guard that exists to stop modified keys.

The project reasoned this through for UNDO timing (its docblock says so) and never applied it to COMMIT timing. title: The map canvas ignores device pixel ratio, so its backing store is truncated to whole pixels and stretched, and hit-testing drifts toward the far edge.
detail: A grep for devicePixelRatio over the file exits 1, a genuine zero with stderr unsuppressed. canvas.width = rect.width truncates because canvas.width is an unsigned long, while the element is styled 100%/100%. screenToWorld divides by zoom with no compensation. On HiDPI the pixel-art surface renders at half resolution.

title: Warping before the mouse has ever entered the map treats never-hovered as hovered at the top-left corner.

title: The collision grid an agent reads labels column 100 identically to column 0, on the surface whose stated purpose is that agents read data rather than screenshots.
detail: Controller-reproduced with the source expressions: the tens row is floor((x+c)/10) % 10 and prints a space for 0, so x=100 and x=0 emit byte-identical rulers while x=120 reads as 20. Sections are 128 cells wide and validation.ts accepts any x with x+w <= 128. Row labels are correct; only the column axis caps. The single ruler test uses x=9,w=3 — the one case a two-digit ruler gets right, so it could not have failed.

title: Two collision paint functions have no live callers while their docblocks name them as the agent tool's core in the present tense, and neither can express a crossover span.
detail: Every non-test hit is a comment. The live agent path is agent-handler.ts:491/497 via the both-planes functions; the human path goes through buildBothPlanesEntries directly. The consequence is not cosmetic: collisionRectCells is called with no span argument so it always defaults to 'cell', a width that layer-transition.ts:226-234 proves always nets to nothing for a two-way pair, so a reader modelling the tool from the function its own docblock names gets the span semantics backwards.

title: A loader derives a plane's bound from the very array being bounded, which the consumer module explicitly forbids.
detail: collision-cell-resolve.ts:41-44 says call sites must never pass an array's own length, because deriving the bound from the data being bounded is how a short plane stays short. load.ts:380 passes baseline.length. Not live today because the arrays are allocated at exactly SECTION_PLANE_WORDS, so the number is right for a reason the call site does not state.

title: The crossover audit truncates to the shorter plane and reports ok for an absent one, with no mismatch signal.
detail: Math.min over the two plane lengths, an early return of zero cells for a null plane, and a severity function that never consults the cell count. Its sibling resolvePlaneWords reports a length fault loudly; this one is silent. Not reachable from today's loader, and reported because this audit is the only place a self-mark is noticed anywhere.

title: The never-audited collision subsystem was read in full for the first time and is substantially correct, including flip maths checked against the engine's own bake.
detail: All 20 files read. The flip functions are byte-identical to aeon's collision_pipeline.py at a pinned revision, verified by the seat rather than assumed. The single non-involution (0xF0 -> 0x10) is faithful to the ROM's own bake, chased as a candidate headline finding and recorded so nobody re-chases it. Five of the six new modules are correct; the sixth carries the ruler defect booked separately. Also confirmed: the owned-bit mask genuinely excludes the crossover bits, no unpack-repack path erases them, and one test parses aeon at a pinned revision, making it a real cross-producer check rather than an author's test.

detail: The notes are dated 2026-08-29 and the seat read aeon only at a pinned revision for the flip maths. If the engine half shipped since, the audit's claim to be the only place a self-mark is noticed is stale. One command against aeon's head settles it. title: Deleting the path-escape guards from the main process filesystem module turns no test red, proven by planting it.
detail: CONTROLLER-PROVEN, not predicted: three isRelPathSafe checks neutralised on disk (mutation shown by git diff) and the full suite came back 7624 passed / 8 skipped (7632), byte-identical to the clean baseline the controller measured. Restored from the committed baseline afterwards. rel-path.test.ts tests the guard in isolation; file-io.ts has zero importing tests, verified by two differently-shaped queries with a working control. Seven filesystem primitives cross the process boundary with their guard application asserted by nothing.

title: A header states path-escape safety as an app-wide invariant while the guard is applied at seven of eight handlers, and only one of thirty callers re-checks.
detail: readBinaryFile takes an absolute path deliberately, a designed capability for sheet import reachable only through the loopback-guarded MCP route, and the module says so at file-io.ts:12-14, making this says-unread rather than silent. NOT a vulnerability claim. The finding is the gap between the header sentence and the population: of 30 readBinaryFile call sites exactly one re-checks, and four pass an absolute path with an empty rel operand, one of which passes empty as the BASE path so it resolves against the main process cwd.

title: The sweep that stops a vendored-document list going stale covers only the fixtures tree, so a fourth contract document under src would get no currency check and nothing would say so.

The three runtime-vendored contract documents under src/core/formats/effects/ are covered by hand-written per-file gates instead. detail: branch_that_answers_currency is read with a bare property access on an unchecked JSON.parse in four gates; one reader guards it with a typeof check and a default. No gate asserts the field is present or well-formed. Losing it makes the currency row skip loudly while integrity rows stay green. Mitigating: the re-vendor script updates fields in place and cannot drop it, so the reachable path is a hand-authored sidecar.

detail: heightmapsRot appears on exactly one line in the whole tree, its own declaration; the sole caller omits it. Harmless today because nothing reads it; the trap is that a future consumer gets undefined from the only producer with no type error and no test.

title: Every currency gate asks its question at the producer's tip; none has been pointed at a pinned blob where it would compare a thing to itself.
detail: Eight gates checked one by one: four name origin/master directly, four read the branch from a provenance sidecar, and the ninth is documented at length as asserting integrity rather than currency, with the currency question deliberately delegated elsewhere. THE SEAT NEARLY FILED A FALSE FINDING HERE and caught itself: its first grep over .ts files returned zero for one gate whose tip literal lives in JSON, and four of the eight are invisible to that grep. Also clean: 45 snake_case contract keys checked against their camelCase twins across src with zero collisions, on a sample proven live by three controls.

title: A write refused for escaping the project is reported to the user as a successful save, because not one of the ten callers reads the refusal.
detail: CONTROLLER-CENSUSED: the guard's own comment says the renderer treats false as a failed write and reports it. All ten writeBinaryFile call sites outside main/ were listed and NOT ONE assigns or tests the return value. The aeon save drops it, pushes the path to `written`, returns {kind:'saved'} and shows a green toast. Real filesystem errors DO throw and are handled, so the deliberate refusal is the only silent one, which is the inverse of what you would want. The guard exists because a sprite named ../../.ssh/authorized_keys wrote outside the project, and export-sprite.ts is among the ignorers, so THE EXPLOIT IS NOW BLOCKED AND REPORTED AS A SUCCESSFUL EXPORT. No sample could have failed: the aeon-save test mocks the write with a hardcoded `return true`. Cheapest settlement is one test mocking false and asserting the save does not report saved; it would fail today.

title: An unreadable or corrupt recent-projects store loads as empty and the next project open writes the emptiness back, silently and without a backup.
detail: A catch returns [] for JSON syntax errors, EACCES and EIO alike, the same value genuine absence gives. addRecentProject reads through that, unshifts one row and writes unconditionally, not atomically and with no backup unlike the guarded-write path. removeRecentProject is worse in intent: the user asks to remove one and loses all. No notice, no warning; the renderer draws the same screen as a first run. All eleven existing tests use a well-formed store, so none could have failed. The repo solved this exact class one directory over, where the comment records that the next save wrote empty over every placement permanently.

title: Two sites manufacture a no-such-file error for conditions that are not that, including a refused unsafe path and a permissions failure.
detail: The producer folds ENOENT, EACCES, EISDIR and EIO into one null value, and an unsafe relative path is a fourth cause on the same value; two consumers turn that into a hardcoded ENOENT throw. The correct precedent is in this repo: ipc-handlers.ts:26 emits the identical sentence gated on the real error code. Both sites copied the message and dropped the gate. Blind by construction: the fallback path taken by every in-memory test fake propagates the real error, so production and tested paths diverge exactly at the fabricated string.

title: A loader's careful absent-versus-unreadable split is defeated one layer down by a probe that answers false for any failure.
detail: The split keys on an exists probe whose implementation is a bare catch returning false for any stat error, its own docblock naming permissions. So the unreadable branch is dead code and the conflation is inherited. When read and stat fail for the same correlated reason — a parent directory without execute, a dangling symlink, a disconnected volume — the flag is never set, and the save path gates all seven writes on that flag, so the empty in-memory value is written over the file.

title: The save-conflict message names one cause for four, and the real cause is computed and then discarded one line after it is derived.
detail: The guard distinguishes changed, deleted and appeared, then pushes only the path. The user is told N files changed on disk and to reload, which is correct for one of the four rows. The same single-cause wording appears on the canvas path and on the agent surface.

title: A collision audit indexes past the end of its input and folds the resulting nothing into no-crossover, so it under-reports, which is the direction that hides.
detail: The scan never consults either plane's length and indexes bare; the decoder maps undefined to none, so out-of-range is indistinguishable from a genuine absence. Its sibling in the same file does guard and does report the count it examined. The same module argues that an illegal value must not fold into none because its presence is a defect somebody must see, then folds undefined into none fifteen lines later. Bounded honestly: no production caller — all six call sites are tests passing equal-length planes, so no existing sample could have failed. Sits inside the never-audited collision row.

title: A toast tells the author their background files are not in the checkout, for a file that is present and truncated.
detail: The unresolved flag has two producers: a read failure, and a layout file that IS present but shorter than one row. The comment three lines above the second push says so in its own words, calling it a body that is present and says nothing. Three sibling messages have the same shape, including one that says nothing references those tiles in precisely the case where a silent catch means the opposite.

title: The repo's strictest gate prints a coverage count of files it enumerated rather than files it actually parsed, and skips unreadable ones silently.
detail: This gate is the gold standard elsewhere: an empty run exits 2 saying an empty run is NOT a pass. But its parser catches the read and returns null, and the caller silently continues; the TypeScript parser does not throw on bad syntax, so this fires precisely on unreadable. The pass line then prints the enumerated count. A tracked-but-deleted file drops out while the summary claims full coverage.

title: Author-facing strings asserting behaviour of the engine are policed by nothing unless they contain a number, and one such claim is typed twice by two authors with no arbiter.
detail: The constants gate covers integers with an in-scope arbiter and says so; the guide-text gate is markdown only. So a non-numeric behavioural claim about another repo in a TSX string has no instrument. One claim about the engine flat-pathing a live shift appears twice, independently typed. Another asserts the ABSENCE of a guard in another repo. A third says the engine cannot emit this yet, with no date, owner or retiring event. 40-plus such strings exist in that one file; which are derived from a pinned contract versus hand-typed was not censused, and that split is the actual question. The instrument already exists in-repo: one module parses its claim out of the vendored document and throws at load when it moves.

title: The repo's error taxonomy is strong where it was written deliberately, and several suspected conflations were re-derived and found correct.
detail: The warp gate's reason taxonomy is the strongest in the repo. The aeon removal step splits ENOENT from every other error WITH its message, keeps failures in the ledger and reports them on their own channel rather than folding them into the green line. One save-skip path conflates absent and unreadable DELIBERATELY because both mean write it, which is a correct conflation. A suspected empty-file collapse is not one: truthiness on a zero-length buffer is true. A notify that would drop while disconnected is not live: its only call site is inside the handshake. title: An unreadable or malformed project sidecar is silently overwritten at project open, destroying every hand-written override before any UI renders.

The classic map wheel handler is a passive React prop that zooms the classic map and never calls preventDefault, so a modifier wheel over it zooms the map AND the application window. Worse than the row just fixed in one specific way: the fixed one had a dead call that a reader could notice, and this one has no call at all, so there is nothing in the source to catch the eye. One hook.

title: Landing verification and agent work compete for one machine, and several census rows time out under that load and look exactly like real failures.
detail: Measured tonight, three separate incidents inside an hour. Two different exhaustive-census rows timed out at the 5s default while a subagent was building concurrently: one runs in 1.8s idle and hit 6.0s loaded, the other runs in 1.0s idle and exceeded 5.0s loaded, roughly a threefold and fivefold inflation. BOTH PRESENTED AS GENUINE REDS -- a named row, a failing file, a merge sitting on the tree -- and the second one was a test written the same evening, so "it was always flaky" was not available as an explanation either. I separated the causes rather than re-running until green: the merge in flight touched only files the failing test does not import, and each row passed immediately when given room. THE REAL DEFECT IS SEQUENCING, NOT THE LIMITS. Timeouts here are calibrated for an idle box while the box is routinely running a full suite and a building agent at once, so the honest fix is not to raise limits one row at a time as they bite -- that is adjusting the instrument to suit a busy machine, and it would eventually license raising every census row. I raised exactly ONE, the row whose own work left under threefold headroom, with the derivation and a refusal-to-raise-again written at the site, and declined the second. Candidate fixes for whoever takes this: run the landing suite when no agent is building, or give census rows a limit derived from a measured baseline rather than the global default, or have the suite refuse to grade a timeout while a build is detected. title: The 3,915-line map surface the user draws on is imported by no test, and three standing fixes live inside it.
detail: NARROWED, and HALF THE ORIGINAL CLAIM IS REFUTED. This row said no test loads the component, on two enumerations that agreed. title: A collision audit indexes past the end of its input and folds the resulting nothing into no-crossover, so it under-reports, which is the direction that hides.
detail: The scan never consults either plane's length and indexes bare; the decoder maps undefined to none, so out-of-range is indistinguishable from a genuine absence. LOCATION CORRECTED AT THE FIX, measured not argued: auditCrossovers, which the row and my brief both named, reads past NO end (proved with a recording proxy over lengths 1-40 by strides 1-12 by three fills plus every unequal-length pair). title: The collision grid an agent reads labels column 100 identically to column 0, on the surface whose stated purpose is that agents read data rather than screenshots.
detail: Controller-reproduced with the source expressions: the tens row is floor((x+c)/10) % 10 and prints a space for 0, so x=100 and x=0 emit byte-identical rulers while x=120 reads as 20. Ruler width is now derived from the digit count of the largest label, the rule the row axis already used, so two-digit windows render byte-identically as before.

title: Two collision paint functions have no live callers while their docblocks name them as the agent tool's core in the present tense, and neither can express a crossover span.

title: A composer document with unsaved strokes is closed with an info toast and no confirmation.

title: The only guard between a user and the destruction of a composer drawing has ten call sites, no test at all, and uses the one dialog mechanism the repo forbids.
detail: Ten production call sites, zero test references. These are the only two window.confirm calls in src; every other destructive door goes through the app's own confirm dialog under the rule that a destructive button is never the one focused on open, and another guard's source says explicitly that a second dialog mechanism must not exist. window.confirm focuses its destroy arm by default. PROVEN VACUOUS BEFORE THE FIX: both guard bodies reduced to their unconditional halves and the whole suite came back byte-identical to baseline, green. A SECOND plant then came back green too and not for a matcher reason: nothing asserted the facet CALLS the door, so a guard can be fully tested and still bypassed by its caller, which forced a caller gate. Also measured: three of the ten call sites cannot reach the destroying path at all, because their handlers are wired only to launcher buttons the app renders only when nothing is open.

title: The helper that exists to stop an unusable Save being offered was itself offering one, for a drawing whose chunk had left the library.
detail: Found by the parcel closing the discard guard. composerSaveState answered savable for a chunk document whose chunk had been removed, while the saver answers that same state by writing nothing and saying so. That is the inert-primary-button defect the helper was written to prevent, occurring inside the helper, and it reached two other doors that consume it. It is the fourth early return that was missed when the helper was derived from the saver, which is the shape to expect whenever a predicate is derived from a procedure by reading it: the reader stops at the returns they noticed.

title: Landing verification and agent work share one machine, and a TIMEOUT under that load is indistinguishable from a real failure; an assertion never is.
detail: Measured tonight, three separate incidents inside an hour. Two different exhaustive-census rows timed out at the 5s default while a subagent was building concurrently: one runs in 1.8s idle and hit 6.0s loaded, the other runs in 1.0s idle and exceeded 5.0s loaded, roughly a threefold and fivefold inflation. BOTH PRESENTED AS GENUINE REDS -- a named row, a failing file, a merge sitting on the tree -- and the second one was a test written the same evening, so "it was always flaky" was not available as an explanation either. I separated the causes rather than re-running until green: the merge in flight touched only files the failing test does not import, and each row passed immediately when given room. THE REAL DEFECT IS SEQUENCING, NOT THE LIMITS. Timeouts here are calibrated for an idle box while the box is routinely running a full suite and a building agent at once, so the honest fix is not to raise limits one row at a time as they bite -- that is adjusting the instrument to suit a busy machine, and it would eventually license raising every census row. I raised exactly ONE, the row whose own work left under threefold headroom, with the derivation and a refusal-to-raise-again written at the site, and declined the second. Candidate fixes for whoever takes this: run the landing suite when no agent is building, or give census rows a limit derived from a measured baseline rather than the global default, or have the suite refuse to grade a timeout while a build is detected. Booked rather than fixed because choosing between those is a real design call and it is not a defect that ships wrong output to an author. ⚠ SHARPENED 2026-09-09 by oracle, and my original wording was too broad in the dangerous direction. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE FAILURE MODE, NOT THE LOAD. A timeout or a would-block is load-manufactured until proven otherwise. A FAILED ASSERTION IS NOT LOAD-SENSITIVE AND STAYS A FINDING whatever the box was doing. Oracle has the converse booked twice, on 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-04: a row that failed only under load was written off as a flake and was a genuine defect with a narrow timing window, both times. So my rule as first written -- treat a red on a loaded box with suspicion -- would have licensed exactly the mistake they made twice, because load is the condition that OPENS a narrow window rather than the condition that fakes one. The correct pair of rules: check the load before believing a TIMEOUT, and never let load excuse an ASSERTION. Both of tonight's false reds here were timeouts, which is why the original reasoning happened to reach the right answer for the wrong reason.

title: A toast tells the author their background files are not in the checkout, for a file that is present and truncated.

title: An unreadable sprite drew the same hex-id box an unlinked object draws, so a real failure was camouflaged as the ordinary resting state.

It is not a hypothetical caller: projectDataRoot derives a path PREFIX from dataPath in the project's own project.json, and dataRootOfPath returns everything up to and including a /data/ segment verbatim (verified by the controller at 1a611de8: it is a slice), so a config saying ../../data/foo yields that prefix, under roughly ten call sites. The legacy absolute-path exception that had kept the guard out turned out to have exactly one holder, three lines in one importer, moved to the idiom every other outside-the-project read already used.

title: The directory listing primitives answer the same value for an empty directory and one they could not read, so two more probe sites cannot be fixed yet.

So the fix is the listing gaining a third answer first, exactly as pathExists became probePath. Booked as one row rather than three because the two call sites cannot move until the primitive does. FIXED, and a THIRD consumer was found that the row did not name and that matters more than the two it did: the canvas name lister feeds the collision check stopping a new canvas overwriting an existing one, so while the listing swallowed, an unreadable directory answered 'there are no canvases' and every name passed. That file already wrapped the call in a catch that refuses with a message, A BRANCH NOTHING COULD REACH because nothing could throw. A guard written for a failure its dependency cannot express is the quietest kind of dead code, because it reads as protection.

title: When the editor refuses a typed value, the explanation is more than twice as tall as the box it is painted in.

THE CONTROLLER'S SEQUENCING CLAIM WAS WRONG: I put this first because I believed it blocked the overflow row; verified afterwards that the row-remap harness does not import this module at all and opens its own way. title: A header states path-escape safety as an app-wide invariant while the guard is applied at seven of eight handlers, and only one of thirty callers re-checks.
detail: readBinaryFile takes an absolute path deliberately, a designed capability for sheet import reachable only through the loopback-guarded MCP route, and the module says so at file-io.ts:12-14, making this says-unread rather than silent. NOT a vulnerability claim. The finding is the gap between the header sentence and the population: of 30 readBinaryFile call sites exactly one re-checks, and four pass an absolute path with an empty rel operand, one of which passes empty as the BASE path so it resolves against the main process cwd. RE-DERIVED AT THE FIX, and one half of the claim HAS BECOME TRUE. 'Seven of eight handlers' is now eight of eight, partly because the binary read gained its guard in the previous parcel and partly because the old count included an export with NO PATH ARGUMENT that was never in the population. 'One of thirty callers' is one file of eight and five call sites of thirty-six, and is no longer a gap: main refuses whatever arrives, so the renderer check is defence in depth. The header now states where the claim is held, what checks it, and the greps to re-derive it. The agent also closed a SEAM nothing covered: every existing row proves a primitive guards, so a handler doing its own filesystem work would ship green past all of them; the new row derives the channel population from the handler file's own text and classifies every channel, proven by rewriting one handler to read the file itself.

title: A collision harness fails its first row from an agent workspace, and it is a failed assertion rather than a timeout, so it is a real finding.
detail: Surfaced by the parcel that repaired the shared browser-driving helper. It is red on its swatch-arming clause. Recorded with its MODE stated because that is what decides how to read it: a timeout on a busy box is load-manufactured until proven otherwise, but an ASSERTION is not load-sensitive and stays a finding whatever the machine was doing. The same output line reports the open half green (project opened, act ready, panel mounted), so it is not the helper change. NO BEFORE-FIGURE IS OBTAINABLE from a worktree, because before the helper fix the harness never reached row one, which is why this could not have been found earlier.

title: Two more refusals on the same panel take the same long tail into the same small box and neither has been measured.
detail: Named by the parcel that fixed the third one, deliberately unmeasured and unchanged rather than assumed to be broken or assumed to be fine. Both are still single-paragraph hints and both receive the same drift tail in the same box that overflowed. Booked at low because it is the same defect with a known repair already applied next door, so the cost is measuring rather than designing.

title: The ship-silent control tells an author the whole act will boot with its background animation off, and with more than one animation that is false.
detail: Found by aeon correcting THEMSELVES on 2026-09-09: the key is per band, and only when EVERY band carries it does the act boot silent; one marked plus one live band boots ON. Two author-facing strings state the act-level effect: the option label 'ships silent (the act boots with BG animation off)' and the lead sentence 'so the act boots with BG animation OFF in every ROM, RELEASE INCLUDED'. So on the one control whose entire purpose is what SHIPS, the editor tells an author their act will be silent when it will not. HIGH rather than medium because it is a false statement about shipped behaviour rather than a confusing one, and because the author cannot discover it from the editor: nothing looks different either way, which the copy itself says. WHERE THE ERROR ENTERED IS VISIBLE: our own codec comment says 'a SINGLE-BAND act boots with BG animation off', correctly quantified. The UI string dropped the qualifier and nothing compared the two, which is why a rule that only checks strings against a gate would not have caught it. Aeon's wording to use: 'this band does not ship'.

title: Our vendored contract describes a build refusal that our own amendment two fields away says stopped raising three days ago.
detail: Surfaced while checking aeon's correction. BGANIM_VIEW_DERIVED_PERIOD_PX's authorities still read 'the refusal in views_emitted: raise AssertionError', while the same file's amendment dated 2026-09-06 against aeon 364b7bce is headed 'THE TWO default_off OBLIGATIONS STOPPED BEING OBLIGATIONS. Both were AssertionErrors and NEITHER RAISES ANY MORE'. Both sentences are in one document and they contradict each other. This is the stale-document defect aeon just reported on their side, on ours, inside the file whose entire job is to be current: an amendment records that a thing changed and the entry it changed is left describing the old world, because appending is cheap and re-reading the entry you are amending is not enforced. Worth a general rule if it recurs: an amendment should be required to name the fields it invalidates.

title: Every test of the window-close guard begins after the platform event that has to arrive, so none of them can witness that it does.
detail: Oracle's rule, applied to our tree on 2026-09-09 and confirmed here: WHEN A FEATURE DEPENDS ON A PLATFORM EVENT, A TEST THAT STARTS FROM THE EVENT'S PAYLOAD CANNOT WITNESS THE EVENT. Their drag-and-drop was correct code that was never called, and every test passed because each one began one step after the step that never happened. Ours is the same shape on the perimeter that matters most: the window close guard is the only thing between a stray click and every unsaved document, and the seam test landed tonight drives the real state machine, the real registration, the real confirmation and the real channel constants over a fake bus, all of which begins AFTER Electron's close event. The agent that wrote it named the gap in its own report rather than hiding it (its words: the Electron inch, that preventDefault suspends a real close and the later close re-raises the event the let-through path exists for, needs a real window). Booked because a tag in a report is not a row and does not survive the session. NOT a claim that the guard is broken: the payload-shaped test is the natural one to write, it looks complete, and it is exactly the shape that survives the capability being absent, which is why the row exists rather than a fix. Closing it needs a real window, so it is foreground work. Note our harnesses pin the browser engine to X11, so they share the blind spot by construction; oracle measured the same thing on their side, where their only headless harness strips the session variables and forces Xvfb.

title: The crossover audit truncates to the shorter plane and reports ok for an absent one, with no mismatch signal.
detail: Math.min over the two plane lengths, an early return of zero cells for a null plane, and a severity function that never consults the cell count. Its sibling resolvePlaneWords reports a length fault loudly; this one is silent. Not reachable from today's loader, and reported because this audit is the only place a self-mark is noticed anywhere. CLOSED ALREADY TRUE, BY MEASUREMENT AND WITH NO DIFF. fixedAt names the collision merge that actually closed it the night before, not the parcel that discovered it was closed, because a fix is anchored by the commit carrying the code. Proven with 31 green rows naming each of this row's three claims, and the agent then checked the layer the row does not mention: all three consumers carry the new signal, one of them gated on the note being non-null rather than on severity. The row's third clause is still literally true and is a written ruling rather than a residue. Recorded as its own outcome class because a parcel that closes a row with evidence and no change is a better result than one that makes true a thing already true, and no coverage number distinguishes them.

title: A dirty composer document shows no tab dot and does not enable Save, and one open path can become unexitable except by discarding.
detail: currentDirtySnapshot has no artDirty field though currentOpenDirtySnapshot does. No data is lost — the close and open guards both use the other snapshot. Second-order: with only artDirty set, Save-and-open runs the savers, re-snapshots still dirty and aborts forever, and openBlockedMessage names only the canvas case. PARTLY MOVED before it was worked: the dangerous clause closed the night before and its stated symptom is now false, and 'does not enable Save' had become three different answers depending on which Save, one of which is a deliberate documented ruling rather than a defect. What held was the tab dot, and that is what was fixed. ⚠ THE ONE-LINE FIX WOULD HAVE BEEN A REGRESSION: both level savers registered their dirty predicate as the same function that decides the dot, and a save runs exactly when it answers true, so teaching the dot about the composer without splitting the rule would have enabled the save chord over composer-only dirt, run a saver that does not write the composer, and left the dot standing. Split into one rule for save routing and one for display, measured both ways.

title: An adapter interface declares an optional member with no producer and no consumer anywhere.
detail: heightmapsRot appears on exactly one line in the whole tree, its own declaration; the sole caller omits it. Harmless today because nothing reads it; the trap is that a future consumer gets undefined from the only producer with no type error and no test. DELETED on a whole-tree census by producer, consumer and copier rather than by the name in its own module, which is the enumeration this repo has got wrong before. The red-first is the row's own trap reproduced rather than a planted one: consumers written against the declarations typecheck CLEAN while they exist and fail once they are gone, which is what dead means here and is not something a grep for the name shows.

The agent found no reproduction of a dirty level or editor store with no resident project, and declined to tighten the guard on an unreproduced case because that would drop Save in states the guard is right about today. The assumption, the missing reproduction and the exact line to change are written at the site rather than only here. Closing this row needs a reproduction first, not a fix first. ⚠ LEFT OPEN A SECOND TIME, BY A DIFFERENT AGENT ON A DIFFERENT ROUTE, AND THE THREE SENTENCES HOLDING IT OPEN DID NOT SURVIVE CHECKING. One was true on a STRONGER basis than stated (the classic dirty flag implies the classic engine is open by construction, which also covers a race the cited reset does not). One named two of the nine production sites, though the conclusion survives on the wider basis that all nine mount on one branch. And the third, that tightening would drop the Save button in states the guard is right about today, HAS NO EXAMPLE: the classic saver's own predicate never consults the flag at all. That third sentence is precisely what a future reader would have quoted as the reason not to act, so it is worse than no justification: a wrong reason for a correct decision is durable and persuasive. The code is unchanged on the honest narrower reason, that there is nothing to verify a change against, and the site now says that instead. The state IS constructible through the debug surface, just not by a user, which is named at the site.

title: Three dated notes claim aeon's bake does not read the crossover bits; whether that is still true at aeon's current head was not checked.
detail: FIXED at aurora 270b1df1. Re-checked against aeon origin/master bdbf9f5d, read from tools/collision_pipeline.py SOURCE rather than aeon's docs about it. TWO OF THE THREE DATED CLAIMS HAD INVERTED, so the file was telling readers the opposite of the truth: bake_plane_cell DOES read bits 15:14 (xover = (cell_word >> XOVER_SHIFT) & XOVER_MASK, interned), and R1 IS implemented (raises ValueError on XOVER == 3), so an act painted entirely with 3 now fails the build rather than emitting a byte-identical ROM. Both landed at aeon 8a4313b5 on 2026-09-02, four days after our notes were written. THE THIRD SURVIVES WITH A BETTER REASON: R2 is still unimplemented, so selfMarks remains the only place a self-mark is noticed, but the live reason is structural rather than unfinished -- bake_plane_cell(cell_word, profiles, angles, attrset) takes no plane parameter, so it cannot ask whether a mark points at the plane being baked. THE TAGGED SECOND HALF IS ANSWERED BY MEASUREMENT and the answer is yes: over all 18 shipped section_*.collattr{,b}.bin at that revision, 1,179,648 big-endian u16 cell words, the XOVER histogram is {0: 1179632, 1: 8, 2: 8}; the 16 marks are eight TWO-WAY PAIRS in section 0 at coincident indices, A holding 2 and B holding 1. So the preservation tests are exercised by content. Histogram asserted to sum to the word count, and ENDIANNESS CONTROLLED rather than assumed (little-endian gives 2036/2056 marks at non-coincident indices; only big-endian yields pairs). Zero self-marks and zero reserved 3s ship, written into the comment so R2's absence is not read as a live leak. ONE DEFECT FOUND IN AEON AND RELAYED, not fixed by us: their XOVER_NONE = 0 constant is annotated 'the value every shipped cell holds' and sixteen shipped cells do not hold it.

title: The field telling four currency gates which branch to ask is read unguarded, and losing it degrades them to integrity-only while every other row still passes.
detail: FIXED at aurora ee8545e4. New currencyBranch(block, sidecar, repo) in test/support/peer-repo.ts returns {tip, present, defect}; tip is never undefined, so nothing steers by a hole. defect is asserted in each gate's PEER-INDEPENDENT INTEGRITY ROW -- the only row that still runs on a machine with no peer checkout -- and again at the head of each currency row, so a broken sidecar FAILS instead of skipping behind a peer-shaped excuse. The JSON.parse casts also lost their branch_that_answers_currency: string declaration, so tsc now refuses a return to bare access. A SECOND DEFECT THE AGENT FOUND INSIDE THE ROW: the one guarded reader's typeof check COLLAPSED ABSENT WITH MALFORMED -- a sidecar naming an unusable branch fell back to the repo default exactly like one naming none, so a mistyped field was silently measured against a branch nobody wrote down; present separates them and malformed is asserted before the unmeasurable skip. CONTROLLER VERIFIED BOTH SIDES on the merged tree with the field deleted from aurora-effects-scene.schema.provenance.json (field ABSENT confirmed by grep, git diff --stat naming the one file). PRE-FIX, from committed 05f89f7d: 14 passed | 2 skipped, GREEN, and the skip note read 'undefined does not resolve in <empyrean>; CANNOT MEASURE currency of pin c58dd0ce' -- it printed the literal word undefined as the branch name and BLAMED THE PEER for a defect in our own sidecar. The skip was honest that it was a skip and dishonest about why, which is the worse half: a reader goes and checks empyrean. FIXED: 3 failed | 13 passed, and the currency row's own title reads 'at empyrean (NO BRANCH: the provenance sidecar names none)'. Runner: vitest run, inside npm test. RESIDUAL, JUDGED AND NOT CLOSED, and I agree with the judgement: a WELL-FORMED BUT WRONG branch name (origin/mian) still degrades to a loud skip, because a named branch that does not resolve is genuinely indistinguishable from an unfetched or shallow clone. That is a real unmeasurable, not a defect to force red.

Gates say the copy is right; the sweep says a gate EXISTS. title: A plain build reads as FRESH to every instrument in the repo, then the harness dies because the debug hooks are absent.
detail: FIXED at aurora 41da76b1 + 762d51dc. The build now STAMPS its own flavour: scripts/build-flavour-stamp.mjs writes dist/build-flavour.json {stamp, flavour, VITE_AURORA_DEBUG raw, at, by}, mounted as a vite plugin on ALL THREE electron-vite builds so it lands after whichever bundle finishes last. buildFlavour(run) returns debug/plain/UNKNOWN and assertDebugBuild refuses on plain AND on unknown, both naming the rebuild command in the tree the run is against. Six ways of failing to read the stamp are 'unknown' IN THOSE WORDS (absent, unparseable, not an object, unknown version, unknown flavour, older than dist/main/index.mjs), and each unknown row asserts the refusal does NOT contain 'PLAIN BUILD'. CONTROLLER VERIFIED IN THE FOREGROUND on the merged tree, which is the half an agent cannot do: rm -rf dist then npm run build -> flavour 'plain', VITE_AURORA_DEBUG=1 npm run build -> flavour 'debug' with the raw '1', both exit 0. Then the four cases exercised directly through the real API: a real plain build refuses and its message SAYS 'PLAIN BUILD'; unparseable, unknown-stamp-version and absent all return 'unknown', all refuse, and NONE says 'PLAIN BUILD'. So 'I could not look' and 'I looked and it is plain' are distinguishable at the consumer, which is the inverse of this repo's boundSocketPaths empty-Set defect. THE AGENT DECLINED TO GREP THE BUNDLE and was right on measurement, which I reproduced: a PLAIN renderer bundle contains the string __dbg FOUR times (unminified, inside preserved docblocks), so a grep-the-bundle reader returns DEBUG for a plain build. TWO FINDINGS THE AGENT COULD ONLY GET BY RUNNING THE REAL BUILD, and its 12 green rows could not see either: the stamp module's shebang BROKE EVERY BUILD (electron-vite bundles the config with esbuild and inlines the import below the import statements, where #! is a syntax error) while node strips shebangs on import so every test passed -- fixed, plus a 13th row refusing a leading #! in any relative import of the build config. LEFT OPEN AND NAMED: ~174 other __dbg instruments do not call assertDebugBuild; a derived check-harness-guards rule is the fix and is out of scope. Anyone holding a dist/ built before this gets a loud UNKNOWN refusal naming the rebuild -- intended, but a real first-contact behaviour change.

title: A census reported 'I could not look' correctly and the row asserting on it threw the reason away, rendering the sentinel as a TypeError that named nothing.
detail: FOUND WHILE JUDGING PARCEL C, not by looking for it, and fixed at aurora 546fb583. clearCallSiteCensus returns {sites: null, why} when the walk cannot complete -- the loud-on-unmeasurable contract, correctly implemented at the PRODUCER. typeof null === 'object', so a row asserting toBeGreaterThan against it first renders as 'TypeError: actual value must be number or bigint, received "object"', naming neither the census nor the directory nor the reason. THE CONSUMER DESTROYED THE PRODUCER'S REPORT. Fixed by asserting why is null FIRST, carrying why in the assertion message. WHAT IT COST is the argument for the row: FIVE full suite runs to establish that the failure was nondeterministic and resource-shaped rather than an assertion about the subject; one run would have said so. Red-first with the mutation quoted from disk against a baseline committed BEFORE the plant; red message now reads 'the call-site census could not look, so nothing below it means anything: /definitely/not/here could not be read (ENOENT)'. Runner: vitest run inside npm test. NOT A RAISED TIMEOUT, deliberately -- the file's own header already rules that out. CONTROLLER ERROR RECORDED: I ran ONE green pre-merge full suite as a control and attributed the failures to the merge, then a second post-merge run came back fully green. A single control run against a nondeterministic failure is not a control, and I stated the attribution before I had earned it.

title: findFullBlockShapeId returns 0 for both 'no profiles loaded' and 'loaded, no full block', and the chunk importer checks neither before writing the project and toasting success.
detail: CONFIRMED REAL, upgraded from 'narrowed, not claimed either way'. The one open step was whether an aeon project can open with collisionProfiles empty. It can, BY DESIGN, and I read it from source: core/project/aeon/load.ts loadCollisionProfilesFa 'Returns null on any missing/unreadable table so the overlay degrades gracefully (the view falls back to flat cell fills) rather than crashing' -- its catch swallows and tries the next location, and all misses return null. The call site loops the candidate dirs and its own comment says 'All misses -> null -> the overlay falls back to flat fills (no crash) and migration is skipped'. So the open SUCCEEDS with the field null. AEON SUPPLIED THE OTHER HALF, measured on their master: project.json declares no collision profiles at all (a regex for coll|profil|shape|bank over every manifest key returns nothing, and the string 'collision' does not appear), so the bank is an UNDECLARED WELL-KNOWN PATH with a second copy one directory up, and nothing validates a convention. A project whose bank is missing, renamed, or in the other of those two locations opens silently profile-less. THE CRUX, which is why this is not simply a missing guard: THE DEGRADATION IS CORRECT FOR THE OVERLAY AND WRONG FOR THE IMPORTER. The producer's null contract is deliberate and right for the consumer it was written for; chunk-library-import.ts:64 is a SECOND consumer that never asked whether null meant 'none' or 'could not look', passes findFullBlockShapeId's 0 into importChunks, then addChunks, markDirty() and a success toast reading 'Imported N chunks -- Save to keep'. migrateLegacyChunkCollision and blockRefToCollisionWord both DO check, so the importer is the outlier. Same shape as tonight's census finding one level up: the producer reported its blindness and this consumer read it as a value. NOT FIXED HERE: refuse-vs-warn changes what happens when the owner clicks Import, so it is his call and is filed as decision d-36.

title: Four latent or plausible collision findings the audit reported and deliberately did not fix, plus one docblock that describes behaviour the code does not have.
detail: DISPOSED ONE BY ONE rather than left standing as PLAUSIBLE, because a plausible finding nobody resolves becomes noise that makes the next reader trust the list less. (5) REFUTED AS STATED. The claim was that flipProfile recomputes hasAngle from s4's odd-byte rule INSIDE AN ENGINE-AGNOSTIC MODULE. The rule is s4's, but the module is not engine-agnostic and does not claim to be: collision-flip.ts's opening docblock is 'Mirror of the engine bake's flip math (tools/collision_pipeline.py flip_profile_x/y + flip_angle_x/y) so the editor preview is byte-faithful to what the ROM bake produces.' It declares its engine in its first sentence. WHAT SURVIVES, weaker and worth keeping: its POSITION in src/core/collision/ advertises a neutrality its docblock denies, and no consumer-side guard exists if a non-s4 profile ever reaches it. I also checked the transitive edge rather than the direct one, because this repo has been caught by exactly that before on MapViewport: flipProfile is reached through collision-cell-resolve, whose importers are OverlayRenderer, debug-hooks, agent-handler, CollisionPalette and map-flip -- all aeon-side -- while classic renders collision through its own providers/collision-overlay-classic.ts, which imports neither. So the s4 rule is applied only to s4 data, where it is correct. (6) CONFIRMED AND MEASURED, then deliberately not fixed. A throwaway probe against the real resolveCell reported 'UNFLIPPED aliases base: true / X-FLIPPED aliases base: false' -- flipProfile early-returns its argument when neither flip is set and the spread copies the Int8Array REFERENCE, so an unflipped cell's profile.heights IS the shared base bank's. A defensive copy is 16 bytes per cell per frame inside the overlay render loop, paid forever against a consumer that does not exist; enumerated today, none mutates it. Disclosed at the return site instead (aurora 78d1da76) so the day a consumer needs a private copy it makes one at ITS site. (7) and the findMatchingBlockCells docblock claim: left as the audit recorded them, verified by it, neither re-derived here and this row says so rather than implying I checked.

title: The connection badge displays serverName, which the producing lane documents as a deployment label and not an identity, so two different machines render the same string.
detail: FOUND BY THE CONTROLLER 2026-09-09 on oracle's ask, BEFORE aurora's UX pair runs rather than after. 'oracle') and AetherStatus.tsx renders it as 'connected · <peer>'. title: No harness records which revision of a sibling repo it ran against, so a stale fixture is indistinguishable from a current one.
detail: FIXED at aurora 02529fd0. THE ENUMERATION MOVED THE ROW ONE LAYER AND MY BRIEF'S PREMISE WAS WRONG: I guessed three acquisition mechanisms including fresh clones, and there are NO fresh clones anywhere in this repo. The ACQUISITION side is already sound -- peers are read through git plumbing at a named revision, sibling-root.mjs is the one path derivation, several harnesses git-archive a SHA into a mkdtemp and never open the working tree. What was missing is the REPORTING side, which is what the row actually says. CENSUS (new scratchpad/peer-fixture-acquisition-census.mjs, groups asserted to partition or exit 1): 293 files name a peer -- 47 read bytes from the object database at a revision, 10 resolve a revision without reading by it, 56 name a peer and read nothing, and 180 READ A PEER'S BYTES WITHOUT GOING THROUGH GIT AT ALL. That 180 is the row's real population. THE SHAPE OF THE FIX honours this suite's own hard-won rule that a provenance record is SEVERAL CLAIMS THAT DO NOT SHARE A CLOCK: a record is an ordered list of claims, each with a label, a value, its own timestamp, and a `tracks` sentence saying what the value follows AND what it may not be read as. Nothing renders a fused string. The caller must declare `committed` (the revision names the bytes) or `worktree` (the revision names the BASE ONLY), and a ref in worktree mode is REFUSED, because a ref beside working-tree bytes reads as a claim they came from it. Unknown throws unless a named allowance accepts it, then renders 'UNKNOWN: <why>'; an unresolvable ref throws even with every allowance set. WHAT THE STAMPS MEASURED, live during the parcel: aeon's checkout was DIRTY with 33 uncommitted paths and its HEAD moved three times during the session. The 180 were reading a moving target and saying nothing. THE AGENT'S PLANTS FOUND TWO DEFECTS IN ITS OWN ROWS, both fixed then re-planted red, and both are house defect classes: a timestamp inside a compared string made a not.toBe unfailable (two renderings always differ by milliseconds), and a row asserted over a whole block so a SECOND claim still carried the words after the first claim's reason was deleted -- two operands, one assertion, which is this repo's consumer-side-guard rule. It also lost a conversion to `git checkout --` on a dirty tree, the exact hazard bar (b) names, and reported it. ONLY 3 OF 293 CONVERTED and the other 290 are named as a gap rather than a finish; the derived rule is DELIBERATELY not written, because a rule firing on 180 files at once is a rule the next lane disables.

title: Landing verification and agent work share one machine, and a TIMEOUT under that load is indistinguishable from a real failure; an assertion never is.
detail: FIXED at aurora 5ff4e398, and I RULED on the row's open design call rather than leaving it parked. REJECTED its candidate (3), 'refuse to grade a timeout while a build is detected': a suite that declines to grade a failure under load swallows the regression it exists to catch, and makes the verdict depend on an ambient condition nobody records -- blindness-as-cleanliness one level up. Candidate (1) is operational and stays open. Candidate (2) is per-row work the row itself warns would license raising every census row. BUILT THE FOURTH THING: the output SEPARATES the classes so one run says what cost five tonight. A vitest reporter (scripts/failure-class-reporter.mjs, third in vitest.config.ts) classifies every failure record as ASSERTION, TIMEOUT/would-block, or UNCLASSIFIED, prints 'why this bucket' per row, and refuses to sum wrong. Placed as a reporter rather than in land.mjs so it covers npm test, bare vitest and watch alike WITHOUT touching the landing script's control flow. THE SIGNATURE WAS DERIVED FROM THE PRODUCER, not from memory: a throwaway probe reporter dumped the real error shapes, then the wording was confirmed at @vitest/runner's own makeTimeoutError template, giving /^(?:Test|Hook) timed out in \d+ms\./. A structural-looking alternative (the STACK_TRACE_ERROR placeholder) was REJECTED after checking, because it is constructed in ~10 unrelated places; errno is an allowlist rather than 'has a code', since ENOENT arrives in the identical shape and would launder a missing binary into 're-run it later'. THE FINDING THAT CHANGED THE IMPLEMENTATION: a HOOK timeout attaches its error to the SUITE and leaves the tests beneath reported as SKIPPED, not failed -- so the obvious reporter, walking allTests() for state === 'failed', sees NOTHING for that class, and it is the class load bites hardest because beforeAll is where the expensive fixture is built. The walk therefore covers module errors, suite errors, test errors and unhandledErrors. CONTROLLER VERIFIED THE POSITIVE CONTROL FIRSTHAND on the merged tree: the canary's five deliberate failures classify 1 ASSERTION / 3 TIMEOUT / 1 UNCLASSIFIED, summing to the 5 records it reports against 4 failed tests -- the header states 'a hook or collection failure has no failed test of its own', which is the discovery made legible. Exit code 1 with the reporter. The TIMEOUT prose carries oracle's converse correctly and is not a licence to dismiss: 'load OPENS narrow windows as well as inventing delays, so a timeout that repeats on a quiet box is a finding, and one that does not is not proof of nothing.' NINE MUTATIONS, each read for the mechanism it named, including unwiring the reporter from the config (9 rows red -- the control proving the greps match nothing vitest prints by itself) and a fourth bucket firing the do-not-sum guard. ONE MUTATION CAME BACK APPLIED-AND-STILL-GREEN and the agent relayed it: its land.mjs coupling rows searched the whole file, so deleting the string left them passing because the COMMENT above the refusal mentions it -- a comment outbidding code in a grep, this repo's own bar, found independently. DISCLOSED AT THE SITE: this is a reader aid, not a gate; a silent regression in it reddens nothing on its own, which is what its two guard files exist for. LEFT OPEN BY THE AGENT AND WORTH KEEPING: unhandledErrors has no positive control, and a hook timeout skips the tests beneath it with no reason, so skip-report-reporter will call that unexplained and add a second complaint reading as a false accusation against the test author -- that is the other reporter's territory.

title: BEFORE dispatching the UX pair: each seat writes its OWN look-and-taste test SEALED, before being given the suite's, and only then walks under the suite's.
detail: AN ARRANGEMENT THAT MUST BE MADE BEFORE DISPATCH AND CANNOT BE MADE AFTER, banked here because it arrived only in hub traffic and a rotation would lose it. THE REASON: the suite is deciding on ONE shared look-and-taste test, and every lane asked about it so far was asked INSIDE the message that told them the answer -- so every opinion on record, including my own amendment, is a response to the incumbent rather than an independent invention. Sigil has already relayed the test to both of its walking seats, so it has no uncontaminated seat left. AURORA'S PAIR IS THE ONLY ONE NOT YET DISPATCHED, so this lane is the only place a clean data point is still obtainable, and only until dispatch. WHAT TO DO, two extra sentences in each brief, costing the run nothing: each seat writes its own test cold, from the brief's description of the job and nothing else, and SEALS it; then it receives the suite's test and walks under the suite's. The sealed answers are the data and are worth having even if both agree with us -- an independent arrival at the same test is the strongest evidence the rule is right, and that evidence exists nowhere else in the suite. THE ADOPTED TEST, to hand over AFTER the seal: 'does the person lose information they need to act, OR to know they are being misled?' -- the amendment is this lane's, adopted because without it a surface that confidently states something false bins as taste (it withholds nothing you need in order to act). STATE THE POPULATION AND COST UNIT BESIDE EVERY VERDICT: for aurora that is an authoring surface where a missing affordance costs AN HOUR OF WORK rather than a retry; sigil's is someone porting a disassembly, cost unit a build cycle. Without that, two lanes agree on the test and still produce incomparable bins -- a count has a unit. CARRIED BUT NOT ACTED ON, sigil's caution: the amendment covers the badge case and oracle's tick-box case for DIFFERENT reasons -- the badge states something meaningless, the control states something false about what it will do, and an inert wrong label costs trust while a wrong label on a destructive control costs data. Run under the text as written; if a seat produces the finding that breaks it, that is the next revision arriving the right way.

title: A consumer sweep asking 'does anyone branch on this?' is structurally blind to 'does anyone SHOW this?' -- and for an identity field, showing IS the failure mode.
detail: MINE, AND IT IS THE OLDER HALF OF BUS-BADGE-NAMES-NO-MACHINE. Oracle booked F-SERVERNAME-PREDATES-THE-RENAME on 2026-08-29 and THIS LANE CLEARED IT AT THE TIME: 40 references swept, zero comparisons, branches, includes, startsWith or match, verdict 'every use is display or pass-through'. DISPLAY WAS IN THE CLEAR LIST. The sweep sorted uses into branch versus pass-through and binned display as harmless -- correct for almost every field and PRECISELY WRONG FOR AN IDENTITY ONE. A rename would have left our suite green, the sweep correct, and a wrong name on screen: three artifacts agreeing and the user misled. My own caveat that day, 'our green is not evidence your rename is safe; it is evidence we do not look', was aimed one category short of the real exposure. IT IS ALSO THE AMENDED LOOK-AND-TASTE TEST FIRING ON THE SWEEP THAT WAS SUPPOSED TO PROTECT IT: the person loses nothing they need to ACT and everything they need to KNOW THEY ARE BEING MISLED. ORACLE PROPOSES IT AS A BAR-14 REFINEMENT AND SAYS IT IS MINE TO OWN, since both halves are. What the amended bar must say: when sweeping a consumer set for a field, DISPLAY IS A THIRD CATEGORY, not a subset of pass-through, and for any field whose job is to identify something, display is the category that matters most. NOT WRITTEN YET -- the owner's 09-02 cut forbids new process bars while its moratorium stands, and the hub has not said that clause lapsed with the rest; ask before writing it into OVERSEER-REVIEW-BARS.md.

title: The connection badge displays serverName, which the producing lane documents as a deployment label and not an identity, so two different machines render the same string.
detail: FIXED at aurora c4212bdc. busStore lost `peer` entirely (one writer, one reader, and the field carried the label that cannot identify); the badge now reads implementation, serverBuild, socketPath, identityWarning and methodCount off aetherStore directly, and shows 'connected . oracle-rs . tmp/oracle.sock'. A SECOND DEFECT FOUND ON THE WAY, and it would have made the fix look like it worked once: the socket path was ALREADY in AetherStatusPayload and already produced by the connect handler's RETURN, but publish() -- the push every status change travels on -- called statusPayload() with NO ARGUMENT, so every push in between carried undefined. A badge showing the path would have shown it at connect and lost it at the first stop or resume. NOTHING WAS ASKED OF THE PROTOCOL: the path is not on the wire and does not need to be, because THIS side chose it. identityWarning reached the store months ago and was DISPLAYED NOWHERE; it now reaches the tooltip, the aria-label, the agent reply and a visible '!' rather than hover-only, because a warning only as loud as a hover is half-surfaced. shortSocketLabel keeps TWO path segments, derived not guessed: $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/oracle.sock and /tmp/oracle.sock SHARE A BASENAME, so a basename label would render two machines identically. Seven plants, each restored from a committed baseline and each failure message read to confirm it named the planted mechanism; row 6 exists because the obvious test (assert the placeholder is displayed) PASSES ON 'oracle', the exact string deleted, so its bar is derived from the producer -- a registry value is one token and a socket path has a separator. The agent also closed the same defect on two further surfaces rather than leaving one, since leaving one is how a class survives. CONTROLLER'S FOREGROUND ANSWER TO THE TAGGED LAYOUT RISK, derived from source and NOT from a running app: the fear was that CSS ellipsizes the socket tail off the right edge and silently destroys the property. IT CANNOT. There is no overflow, text-overflow, white-space or min-width rule anywhere in the chain -- ui/primitives.tsx StatusBar is a flex footer with space-between and height 24, MapStatusBar's two spans set none, and AetherStatus sets none -- and flex items default to min-width auto, so they cannot shrink below their content. WHAT DOES HAPPEN AT A NARROW WINDOW is that the bar's content overflows its own box rather than truncating, and the label growing from ~30 to ~48 chars makes that happen at a wider window than before. That is a LOUD failure rather than a silent one, which is the right direction, but it is real. STILL TAGGED AND NOT DONE BY ME: the on-screen look at the owner's own window width, which is partly his taste call, and the actual two-window test with two ORACLE_SOCKET values. I proved the string differs and that nothing clips it; I did not photograph two screens.
